name: Beth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a die-cutting press for printed food labels. My vocational certificate covered blade settings and safe stops; I like finding a perfect colour match, but clearing a torn roll from the guarded feed takes patience. I'm experienced and about average on the line, so I still ask the setter to verify tricky dies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular school-kitchen hours. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved. The press role pays above the ordinary operator rate and there are plenty of similar printers nearby. I use AI every day to sort defect logs, then check the pattern against actual sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the label crew the AI log saves me a few minutes finding repeat colour faults, but a printed label still needs the right shade and a clean cut. If the big claims fade, that is fine. Our hands still check the first sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The die-cutting role pays above the usual operator rate, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and my partner has regular hours at a school kitchen. We have two school-age children and a mortgage, but our current wages cover them. There are plenty of similar plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the label die and checking the first printed sheet against the customer sample. I use AI daily to sort defect notes and will keep verifying each suggested pattern against the actual sheets. I'll bring the uneven-colour example to our union shift meeting about paid inspection time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and our finances. I like a tool that saves counting, but I still want a person to sign the sample.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which defect did the log reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday the log showed colour drift on the late run, and the first sheet had a pale corner. We stopped to clean the ink roller before printing the full batch. A label with a pale corner is a real defect, even when the dashboard is green.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the household feel secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nine-month cushion came from years of two wages and careful spending. The mortgage is still there, and we use the school-kitchen rota to plan child pickup. Right now neither job looks like it is disappearing.

say: The **AI defect log** helps find colour drift but cannot approve a printed label.
The crew still needs **first-sheet checks** before a full run.
think: My **higher operator pay** and nine months saved support current bills.
My partner’s **school-kitchen hours** and plentiful local plants add options.
do: **Keep** setting the label die and checking first sheets.
**Bring** the pale-colour sample to the union shift meeting about paid checks.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household income.
S0.quote: A label with a pale corner is a real defect, even when the dashboard is green.
fieldNote: Beth **uses AI daily** to sort defects and checks it against printed samples.
Her **union meeting** concerns paid inspection time; a strong reserve and plentiful local plants support calm.

steps.text: Keep setting label die and inspect first printed sheet
Bring pale-colour label sample to union shift meeting on paid checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shift that AI may write orders and check designs before robots can feed the press. We should get paid time to test any new camera inspection and bargain over its staffing effect. A faster label-inspection report is only useful if fewer bad labels leave the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a new camera quickly, and my higher rate plus nine months saved gives us room. But if the company combines two inspection posts, my own hours could shrink. Plenty of nearby printers helps, yet I do not assume they will match my present wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the next union shift meeting I'll ask for paid trial hours and a written comparison of rejects and crew posts. If the plant offers a guarded paid place with a trainer on camera controls, I'll take it and practise rejecting faulty sample sheets. I'll also learn to use a new AI image-comparison tool on anonymised sample labels and check its errors by eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possibly losing the higher shift rate, but interested in testing the equipment. A certificate will not replace the missing part of a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feed the camera a label with the colour shifted and one with a ragged edge. The trainer should show me how to stop the press safely when it rejects a sheet. I want the test done on paid time before a production target changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shift meeting demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union meeting can compare paid positions before and after the trial, not just rejection counts. If the new plan removes a post, I want notice and a chance to bid on a real trained role. I would ask for the terms in writing.

The crew needs **paid camera trials** and written staffing terms.

Nine months saved and many printers offer time, not **equal wages**.
do: **Ask** union shift for paid trial hours and written crew comparison.
**Practise** guarded camera controls if a paid trainer-led place offered.
**Learn** a new AI image check on anonymous labels and verify errors.
feel: **Anxious** about potential loss of the higher shift rate.
S1.quote: A faster label-inspection report is only useful if fewer bad labels leave the plant.
fieldNote: Her **new AI practice** involves image comparison and error checking, beyond her usual defect-log use.
A **paid guarded camera trial** is conditional on an offered trainer-led place and written crew terms.

steps.text: Raise paid camera trial and crew-post terms at union shift meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the label crew thinking AI could write and check orders by 2028, while capable robots around 2031 could run the press and inspect sheets. I'd ask the union to negotiate notice and offered training before a single post is cut. I won't promise every skilled operator a future role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the physical label work. I expect our crew could lose many posts, including my higher-paid one. Nine months saved and my partner's school-kitchen wage give us a bridge, and there are many local printers, but neither guarantees another job at this rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll put a written staffing and severance proposal on the union branch agenda this month. If the company offers a funded paid-time course in guarded press maintenance with a real practical place, I'll enrol. If my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local printing jobs only if base pay and school pickup work; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local maintenance jobs that meet those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the higher wage, though I have time and places to look. I can ask hard questions without treating a brochure as a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the maintenance course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maintenance test must include locking the die, measuring a worn roller and restarting on scrap sheets with an instructor. If the course is only a video, I would keep looking for a real place. Paid time matters because our mortgage still runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a printing vacancy need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the base rate, not an overtime total, and the shift start against school pickup. A printing vacancy across town is useful only if I can actually work it. If the current rate cannot be matched, we would count the household gap before I applied.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes label orders before capable robots reach presses around 2031.
The union should seek **notice and paid training** before posts disappear.
think: At **48**, I might lose my higher-paid press post.
Nine months saved and **local printers** give options without equal-pay guarantees.
do: **Bring** written notice and wage terms to the union branch.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded press maintenance if practical place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local printing or qualified maintenance if hours cut and pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible loss of the higher wage with workable options.
S2.quote: A printing vacancy across town is useful only if I can actually work it.
fieldNote: She expects **many crew cuts** but has nine months saved, a second wage and multiple nearby plants.
The **printing fallback** and qualified maintenance application each require real safe local posts, base pay and school-compatible shifts.

steps.text: Put written staffing and wage proposal on union branch agenda
Enrol in press maintenance if funded paid guarded practical place offered
Apply to posted safe local printing if hours cut, base pay and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our shift thinking AI could handle label designs in 2031 and capable robots could feed presses around 2034. Five years lets the plant teach maintenance on a real press. I'd ask the union to put offered seats beside a named paid role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when the physical robots arrive. Our children will be older, but the mortgage may still be there. I can grow savings from the higher wage while shifts last; whether I keep earning after training depends on a genuine vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the label press and add new money from each full higher-rate pay month to our reserve after bills. I'll ask the company for covered fees, paid release and guarded hands-on time in a recognized press-maintenance certificate. If it offers a place, I'll enrol; once qualified, if my hours shrink, I'll apply to posted safe local technician roles only if regular pay and travel work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a later crew cut, though five years lets me check a certificate and a job separately. I won't count a course as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would hands-on training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should make me lock the die, adjust a feed roller and run a test sheet before signing me off. I would want that practice on paid time. A press technician who has only watched slides is a danger to the next shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a technician post worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician posting needs its base rate and travel days in writing. Some plants pay more for nights, but school pickup still has to work. I would compare a real offer with our mortgage before leaving the current higher rate.

A **paid training seat** needs a named technical job attached.
think: At **51**, I may still need a mortgage wage.
Full higher-rate months could build **new reserves** before robot staffing changes.

feel: **Anxious** about later crew loss, with time to verify terms.
S3.quote: A press technician who has only watched slides is a danger to the next shift.
fieldNote: Her **new savings** come from future full higher-rate wages, not a shift of existing cash.
The **technician application** follows qualification and reduced hours, and needs posted safe local work with sufficient regular pay and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI might prepare label designs by 2036, and capable robots could run presses around 2039. A decade gives us room to bargain about shorter hours, notice and training before installation. I want actual posts in the agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when robots can do press work. The children may be grown, but I will still need paid work if the mortgage remains. Nine months saved helps us choose, and plentiful local plants make a move possible if their jobs still pay enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the label job and pay extra mortgage principal from new full-wage money after household bills. I'll attend the union branch meeting each quarter to press for paid technical apprenticeships and posted roles. If a funded paid guarded place is offered, I'll take it; after qualifying, if my hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local press-maintenance jobs only when base pay and travel fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant press change. Current shifts pay well, so we can make each move against a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the union agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The branch should ask how many paid operators stay, whether technical seats are offered and who pays their wages during practice. A union agreement without paid operator posts and training wages is a headline, not a plan. I would ask for another meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare a distant job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posting's regular rate with our mortgage, and count the travel hours against family time. A job one hour away at a lower base rate would not suit us. I could keep earning on the present press while checking others.

The union should bargain for **real paid posts** and training places.

Nine months saved and **many local plants** help me assess later openings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut our label-press crew before a technical opening is ready. Written notice, offered funded paid practical training and posted safe local work at a wage we can use would help. I want the union in that discussion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the first printed sheet after a robot changes the die. A label colour can look right on a screen and be wrong on a customer's shelf.

headlineQuote: A label colour can look right on a screen and be wrong on a customer's shelf.
portrait: **Beth**, 43, runs a food-label press with a vocational certificate, higher operator pay and nine months saved.
She and her school-kitchen partner support **two children** and a mortgage, with plentiful similar printers nearby.
Her **progressive outlook** drives real union participation, while daily AI use makes her eager to test new camera controls.
Fast robots leave her **anxious** about losing the higher rate; real training places and posted safe work guide her response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable label-press robots around 2031 before a paid technical post is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid hands-on training and posted safe local work at adequate regular pay would help.
